newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open firm, March trade data due.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open firm, March trade data due.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries prices opened firmer on Wednesday in the aftermath of the Federal Reserve's decision to leave interest rates unchanged and ahead of the release of March U.S. trade data.
March U.S. trade figures are expected to show a similarly sized gap as the deficit reported in February, according to economists polled by Reuters.
The economists estimated, on average, that the U.S. trade gap totaled $10.3 billion in March, versus $10.42 billion in February.
Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds, said the Treasury market would not react directly to the trade data.
Rather, the March trade data could impact the dollar and "that could spill over into the Treasury arena," he said.

"The Treasury market can live with the dollar around the 115 yen level," said Flanagaan. "But if you move closer to 110, then concerns come into play about possible liquidations and that could pose more of a visible problem for our market," he said.
Flanagan said a dollar near 114-115 yen is factored in to Treasury market prices.
"It's when you get to levels with 112 handles, that begins to present some problems," he said.
Flanagan said the market would also look at the monthly federal budget figures for April.
The April budget data, due at 1400 EDT/1800 GMT, is expected to show a surplus of $87.9 billion, according to economists polled by Reuters. In February, the data showed a deficit of $21.32 billion.

"We'll watch the monthly budget statistics," said Flanagan. "They could be interesting given new era of budget detente. We'll take a look at what they could mean for the fiscal situation and supply (of securities). That's something that, over time, could affect how the market trades."

As for how the market will trade in the aftermath of the Fed's decision to leave interest rates unchanged for the time being, Flanagan said, "If the Fed had moved, you would have removed this veil of uncertainty. Now with each economic number we get it will be, 'Yes, they'll tighten in July; no, they won't tighten."
"If the Fed had tightened on Tuesday, most participants would have felt that's probably it for a while," he said.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond traded at 96-10/32 in early dealings, up 4/32 to yield 6.89 percent.
Ten-year notes traded at 99-23/32 initially, up 3/32, to yield 6.66 percent.
Three-month bill rates were 5.08 percent, up one basis point. Six-month rates were up one basis point to 5.27 percent and the year-bill rate was unchanged at 5.47 percent.
Two-year notes were trading at 100-11/32, up 1/32, to yield 6.18 percent.
